topics: 🎯 Aiming for Less, Landing on More — Abaye and Rava on unwitting intent
🔢 Why Count 'Forty Less One'? — Rabbi Yoḥanan on multiple sin-offerings from one lapse
📜 The Mishna of the 39 Melachot — five families of primary labor
🌱 One Melacha, Many Actions — and when two categories overlap
🕳️ Same Action, Different Melacha — how location and purpose decide the label

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Mishna of the Thirty-Nine Melachot
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 73a–73b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out a run of Abaye-Rava disputes about unwitting intent — cases where a person meant to do something permitted but a forbidden result occurred anyway, such as intending to throw an object two cubits but it travels four. It then reaches one of the most famous mishnayot in Shas: the list of the thirty-nine primary categories of labor (avot melachot) forbidden on Shabbat, grouped by function — grain processing, wool and cloth work, leather work, writing, and building/fire/carrying. The Gemara first asks why the mishna bothers to count them, then works through each family, showing how several distinct actions can count as a single melacha, how the same physical act can be classified differently depending on where and why it is done, and where two melachot can be violated by one act at once.

slides.title: 🎯 Aiming for Less, Landing on More
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava dispute several parallel cases

lines.speaker: Case 1
lines.text: One intends to throw an object two cubits in the public domain (no Torah violation) — but it lands four cubits away (a real violation). Liable?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Exempt — he never intended to execute a four-cubit throw, so he had no intent to perform a forbidden act.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Liable — he intended to perform a standard throw, and a throw covering the prohibited distance did occur.

lines.speaker: Case 2
lines.text: One thinks he stands in a private domain and throws far — but it turns out to be the public domain. Liable?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Exempt — same logic: no intent to throw where it is forbidden.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Liable — he intended a standard throw regardless of the domain.

callout.label: Why teach both cases:
callout.text: A third similar dispute — intending to cut a detached plant but severing an attached one — is also needed; none of the three cases can be derived from the others, since the line between a permitted amount and a forbidden one works differently each time.

slides.title: 🔢 Why Count 'Forty Less One'?
slides.subtitle: The tally itself teaches a halakha about multiple sin-offerings

nodes.content: ❓ Why does the mishna bother stating the number, 'forty-less-one'?
💡 Rabbi Yoḥanan: to teach that if one performed ALL of them in a single lapse of awareness, he is liable to a separate sin-offering for EACH ONE

columns.label: Fits Abaye easily
columns.content: He holds one is liable even for a mere error in MEASURE (like the two/four-cubit case) — so full awareness of all 39 categories, with slips only on amounts, is a simple scenario

columns.label: Harder for Rava
columns.content: He exempts measure-errors, so the scenario must be: aware Shabbat forbids labor in principle, yet fully unaware which acts are the forbidden labors — e.g., aware of the sin but not of its karet penalty (R' Yoḥanan), or aware only of the tehum boundary law, per Rabbi Akiva (Reish Lakish)

slides.title: 📜 The Mishna: Thirty-Nine Primary Categories of Labor
slides.subtitle: Grouped by the mishna into five families
rows: Sowing, plowing, reaping, gathering sheaves, threshing, winnowing, selecting, grinding, sifting, kneading, baking

Shearing, whitening, combing, dyeing, spinning, stretching the warp, making two loops, weaving two threads, separating two threads, tying a knot, untying a knot, sewing two stitches, tearing to sew two stitches
Trapping a deer, slaughtering, flaying, salting the hide, tanning it, smoothing it, cutting it to size
Writing two letters, erasing in order to write two letters
Building, dismantling, extinguishing a fire, kindling a fire, striking the final hammer blow, carrying from domain to domain

slides.title: 🌱 One Melacha, Many Actions — Or Two at Once?
slides.subtitle: The sowing-family baraita and its exceptions

boxes.title: One Category, Several Actions
items: Sowing, pruning, planting, bending a branch into the ground, grafting — all ONE melacha (sowing)
Plowing, digging, making a furrow — all ONE melacha (plowing)
Threshing, beating flax, beating cotton — all ONE melacha (threshing)
Doing several of these unwittingly still means only ONE sin-offering

boxes.title: Two Melachot in One Act
items: Pruning a tree needed for its wood: liable twice — reaping (severing) AND planting (Rav Kahana)
Reaping alfalfa for feed: liable twice — reaping AND planting (Rav Yosef)
Cutting beet leaves: liable twice — reaping AND sowing (Abaye)

boxes.title: Exempt
items: Throwing a clod at a palm to knock down dates: Rav Pappa says liable twice (severing + extracting); Rav Ashi exempts — it is not the typical MANNER of either act

slides.title: 🕳️ Same Action, Different Melacha
slides.subtitle: Location and purpose decide which prohibition applies

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Sheshet: had a mound of dirt and leveled it — in the HOUSE, liable for building; in the FIELD, liable for plowing
2️⃣ Rava: had a hole and filled it in — in the HOUSE, liable for building; in the FIELD, liable for plowing
3️⃣ Rabbi Abba: dug a hole only because he needed its DIRT (not to make a hole) — exempt, since digging itself was destructive here, not constructive
4️⃣ Even Rabbi Yehuda, who usually holds one liable for a labor 'not needed for its own sake', agrees here — his stringency applies only to a CONSTRUCTIVE unwanted result, not a destructive one

summary.principle: The mishna's thirty-nine primary labors are not thirty-nine unrelated rules but five functional families, each unified by purpose — so multiple actions within one family count as a single melacha, the same act can fall under different melachot depending on where and why it is done, and true liability always depends on whether the forbidden result was actually intended.

flowSteps.content: 🎯 Unwitting intent: Rava exempts an unintended forbidden amount/domain; Abaye holds intending a standard act suffices
🔢 The count 'forty-less-one' teaches: all 39 in one lapse → liable for each, separately

columns.content: 📜 39 labors in 5 families: grain, wool/cloth, leather, writing, building/fire/carrying
🌱🕳️ Several acts in one family = one melacha; the same act can split across two, or shift by location/purpose

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability on Shabbat tracks the type of constructive act performed and the intent behind it, not merely the physical motion

quiz.q: Why does Rava exempt someone who intended to throw an object two cubits in the public domain, but it landed four cubits away?
o: Because throwing objects is never forbidden on Shabbat
Because he had no intent to execute a throw covering the forbidden four-cubit distance
Because four cubits is not actually a forbidden distance
Because he was in a private domain the whole time
quiz.e: Rava holds that liability requires intent to perform the specific forbidden act; since the person only intended a permitted two-cubit throw, he is exempt even though the result was a forbidden four-cubit throw.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, what does the mishna's tally of 'forty-less-one' primary labors come to teach?
o: That there are exactly 39 verses in the Torah about Shabbat
That if one performs all of these labors in a single lapse of awareness, he is liable to a separate sin-offering for each and every one
That only 39 labors can ever be performed in one day
That the number has no halakhic significance
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that the specific count teaches that unwitting violation of all the primary categories of labor during a single lapse in awareness generates liability for each labor separately, not one collective liability.

quiz.q: How many primary categories of labor (avot melachot) does the mishna list as forbidden on Shabbat?
o: Thirty-six
Thirty-nine
Forty
Forty-two
quiz.e: The mishna states 'avot melachot arba'im chaser achat' — forty-less-one, that is, thirty-nine.

quiz.q: According to Rav Kahana, why is one who prunes a tree specifically because he needs the wood liable to bring TWO sin-offerings?
o: Once for reaping (severing the branch) and once for planting (since pruning stimulates growth)
Once for building and once for plowing
Once for kindling and once for extinguishing
Two sin-offerings are never actually required in Jewish law
quiz.e: Rav Kahana holds that pruning for the wood combines cutting something off (reaping) with encouraging the tree's future growth (planting), making the person liable for both primary categories.

quiz.q: Why does even Rabbi Yehuda agree that one who digs a hole only because he needs its dirt (not to make a hole) is exempt?
o: Because digging is never forbidden on Shabbat
Because Rabbi Yehuda's rule that one is liable for labor 'not needed for its own sake' applies only to a constructive result, and marring the ground this way is destructive
Because he only used his hands, not a tool
Because the amount of dirt removed was too small to count
quiz.e: Rabbi Abba explains that Rabbi Yehuda's stringency about labor performed for an incidental purpose is limited to cases where the physical result is constructive; here the resulting hole is a destructive mark on the ground, so even Rabbi Yehuda exempts it.
